title: How to find dental practices for SaaS sales
summary: Find independent dental practices and qualify them for scheduling, payments, or patient software.
body_markdown:
## TL;DR


For dental software sales, start with practices that match the workflow your product improves. Use business data to build the initial list, then check practice ownership, locations, and the person responsible for evaluating software.


- Define one practice segment and one workflow before building the list.
- Group multiple offices into one account and verify ownership from public sources.
- Use a small outreach test to confirm product fit before expanding the search.


An independent dental practice and a branch of a national dental group can share the same business category while buying software very differently. Start with practice research, then identify who evaluates your product. A directory listing alone does not establish purchasing authority.


This guide is for teams selling scheduling, patient communications, payments, and other practice software. The goal is a small list you can explain and verify before scaling outreach.


## 1. Define the workflow your product improves


“Dental practices in Texas” is a starting market, not a qualified prospect list. Pick a workflow and describe the practice that benefits from it.


For example, a scheduling product might target general dentistry practices in one metro whose websites offer only a phone number or appointment request form. A missing online booking link is a research observation, not proof that the practice lacks scheduling software.


Write down your geography, practice specialty, ownership requirements, and exclusions. Decide whether small groups belong in your target segment or require a separate sales motion.


## 2. Build the business list


Use a business directory or a platform such as[Openmart’s local business database](https://www.openmart.com/products/local-business-database) to begin with practice categories and locations. Review available business profiles, websites, and listed contact details.


Keep one row per account, with locations tracked separately. Two listings with the same domain may represent two offices of one practice. Counting them as two unrelated prospects creates duplicate outreach.


## 3. Verify independence and product fit


Check the practice website, team page, and any publicly disclosed group affiliation. Record the source and date for each conclusion. If ownership remains unclear, label it unknown rather than assuming the practice is independent.


Review the patient journey: appointment requests, intake, payment information, and communication options. Record observable facts. Software usage, budget, and contract renewal dates need confirmation when they are not public.


## 4. Identify the right conversation


Depending on the product and practice, the evaluator could be an owner dentist, practice manager, or operations lead. A listed office phone or shared inbox can help you ask who handles the workflow; it should not be presented as a direct owner contact.


Use this research template:


- **Account and domain:** One practice or group
- **Locations:** Known offices and source
- **Independence:** Confirmed, unclear, or excluded
- **Workflow observation:** Specific public evidence
- **Evaluator:** Confirmed role or unknown
- **Next step:** Verify fit, request introduction, or exclude


## 5. Test a small batch


Review 25 practices before expanding. Measure how many match your criteria, how many have usable business contact routes, and how many conversations confirm the problem you solve.


An opening question can be simple: “I saw your appointment request form and wanted to understand how your team handles requests after hours. Who would be the best person to ask?” Adapt it to what you actually observed.


Start with[Openmart business profiles](https://www.openmart.com/products/local-business-database) , then verify the buying context. A relevant, explainable account list is more useful than a larger list of dental listings.


## 6. Work through a public affiliation example


Heartland Dental’s[May 2026 growth update](https://blog.heartland.com/heartland-dental-monthly-growth-spotlight-may-2026) names Lee’s Summit Family & Cosmetic Dental Care among its newly affiliated supported offices. A familiar local practice name therefore does not establish independence. In your account sheet, record the announced affiliation and its source before choosing the sales route. This example illustrates an ownership check; it is not an Openmart customer or a confirmed software opportunity.


- Account: Lee’s Summit Family & Cosmetic Dental Care.
- Public evidence: named in a Heartland Dental affiliation announcement.
- Research decision: route to group-affiliation review rather than the independent-only segment.
- Still to confirm: who evaluates your specific software category.


Repeat the check for your own practice list. Save the practice domain, organization relationship, source URL, announcement date, and review date. An old announcement supports a historical relationship; verify the current relationship before outreach. For a deeper workflow, read[how to identify DSO-affiliated practices](https://www.openmart.com/blogs/identify-dso-affiliated-dental-practices) .


Keep the segment auditable: unique practice accounts reviewed, accounts matching your criteria, accounts with unresolved affiliation, and conversations that confirm workflow fit. Use the reviewed-account count as the denominator so duplicates do not inflate the result. Compare[dental practice data sources](https://www.openmart.com/blogs/how-to-find-dentist-owner-contacts-best-databases-and-email-lists-2026) when choosing where to assemble your list.


## Recommendation


Start with one metro and one practice type. Use Openmart to research businesses by category and location, then review the practice websites and confirm the relevant evaluator. Test 25 accounts and use the conversations to refine your criteria before building a larger list.

## FAQs


**How do I know whether a practice is independent?**


Check the practice website, ownership disclosures, and any announced group affiliation. Mark ownership as unclear when you cannot verify it.


**Does a missing booking link mean the practice needs scheduling software?**


It gives you a question to investigate. The practice may already use a system that is not visible on its website.


**Who should evaluate dental software?**


The relevant person depends on the workflow and organization. Ask whether the owner dentist, practice manager, or operations team evaluates that category of software.
